items.title: A tsunami can cross the Pacific in under 24 hours
items.claim: How fast does a tsunami travel in deep ocean?

options.text: Around 30 km/h, comparable to wind waves
Around 700-900 km/h in deep ocean (calculated as √(g × depth)) — jet airliner speed; the 1960 Chile tsunami reached Hawaii (10,000 km away) in about 15 hours and Japan in around 22 hours
The speed of sound in water (around 5,400 km/h)
A fixed 100 km/h regardless of depth

items.reveal:
Tsunami speed in open ocean depends on depth: at 4,000 m, around 700 km/h; in 50 m, around 80 km/h. As the wave shoals at coasts, energy compresses vertically and the wave grows from under a metre to potentially tens of metres.

The 1960 Chilean earthquake (M9.5) generated a Pacific-wide tsunami: Hawaii saw 10 m waves around 15 hours later; Japan, 17,000 km away, saw 5 m waves 22 hours after. 142 people died in Japan from a Chilean earthquake.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center (Honolulu, 1949) uses DART buoys (Deep-ocean Assessment and Reporting of Tsunamis) to detect pressure changes from passing waves.
items.why: Distance gives time for warning across ocean basins — but not for nearby coasts. The 2004 Sumatran tsunami killed locally in minutes; Sri Lanka had two hours; Somalia had seven. Warning systems must work at all timescales.

items.title: Tokyo is the world's largest urban area at around 37 million
items.claim: How many megacities exist and which is largest?

options.text: Around 33 megacities (cities over 10 million inhabitants) as of 2022; Tokyo is largest at around 37 million, followed by Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m)

items.reveal:
UN World Urbanization Prospects (2018, updated 2022) lists 33 megacities. Largest by metropolitan area: Tokyo (37 m), Delhi (32 m), Shanghai (28 m), Dhaka (23 m), São Paulo (22 m), Cairo (22 m), Mexico City (22 m), Beijing (21 m), Mumbai (21 m), Osaka (19 m).

Lagos (Nigeria, around 15 m) is the fastest growing — UN projections suggest it could exceed 30 m by 2050. By 2050, around 50 megacities are projected, most in Africa and South Asia.

Definitions matter: 'city proper' versus 'urban agglomeration' versus 'metropolitan area' produce different rankings.
items.why: The geography of global population has shifted. 19th-century urban hierarchies (London, Paris, New York) no longer describe reality. The major cities of the 21st century are largely in countries that were poor a generation ago.

items.title: Gentrification displaces existing residents through rising rents
items.claim: What is the mechanism of gentrification?

options.text: A purely positive process with no losers

Wealthier newcomers move into a previously disinvested neighbourhood; property prices and rents rise; existing lower-income residents (often disproportionately ethnic minority) are displaced — Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explains the economic mechanism
State demolition of all old housing

items.reveal:
Ruth Glass coined 'gentrification' in 1964 in 'London: Aspects of Change', describing the takeover of Islington working-class housing by middle-class incomers. Neil Smith's 'rent gap' theory (1979) explained the economic incentive: the gap between actual rent under disinvestment and potential rent after re-investment attracts capital.

London examples: Notting Hill (1960s onwards), Brixton (2000s), Hackney (2000s-2010s). Berlin: Prenzlauer Berg, Kreuzberg. New York: SoHo, Williamsburg.

Mitigation policies — affordable housing quotas, right-to-return clauses on estate redevelopment, rent control — have variable effectiveness. Sharon Zukin and others have argued the cultural displacement (loss of community) is as significant as the housing displacement.
items.why: Urban regeneration produces winners and losers. 'Rejuvenation' narratives obscure who is being displaced and who the city is being improved for — central to contemporary urban geography.
